title: Hampton, Heywood, rhythm and blues and the Fillmore Four
summary: Royal's recordings after Hite: Hampton, Heywood, blues singers, Little Miss Cornshucks and the Fillmore Four and One More.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: So, your early recording were with Les Height and Louie Armstrong --

After that, I recorded with Lionel Hampton and did a whole series of recordings with them during the time that I was with the band, from 1940 until -- through '42. After that, I went to service. When I came out at the end of service, I went into some recordings with Eddie Haywood (PHONETIC) group. Then I used to record with what they used to call the rhythm and blues groups in those times. That was before the rock and roll stuff. They called them rhythm and blues. And I used to record with various -- all the blues singers and things.

Oh, I can't think of all those folks' names. Percy Mayberry (PHONETIC), Percy Mayfield (PHONETIC) and whoever was the blues things at that time. They had a whole lot of people. Names sometimes escape me, of things that I just did one ortwo times. But you (unintelligible) a lot of unknown people were in the rhythm and blues deals, just the same as they have them now in the rock and roll field. Little Miss Cornshucks --
-- and people like that. She was a great singer.

But -- go through like that. Then during that time, I made a whole series of things with the old Discovery Records with the Fillmore group. I worked with the Fillmore Four out -- right before I went with Basie. They called it the Fillmore Four and One More. I was the "One More."

And we used to work the exclusive clubs on Sunset Strip -- the Mocombo (PHONETIC) and Marcy's Place (PHONETIC) out there and that type of stuff. And during that particular stage, casual recordings and things were coming and going. You never know sometime who you were recording with. You got an unnamed -- they all played the same, so you're not really worried about who it is or where or how. And when you do most of those rhythm and blues recordings, at least the way we did them in those days, after you got through playing so many 12-bar phrases all day, you was just glad to forget the whole thing at the end of the session and look forward to the next one, because they all ended up being the same thing.
